chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter XIII
paragraphs: When Pierre and his wife entered the drawing room, the countess was in one of her usual states in which she needed the mental effort of playing patience. So—though out of habit she greeted him with the words she always used when Pierre or her son returned: "High time, my dear! We've been waiting and waiting. Thank heaven you're here!"—and when she received her presents said the same words she always said: "It's not the gift that counts, my dear... thank you for thinking of an old woman like me..."—it was clear that Pierre's arrival annoyed her at that moment because it distracted her from her unfinished game. She finished the game and only then examined the presents. They consisted of a card box of splendid workmanship, a bright-blue Sevres teacup with shepherdesses painted on it and a lid, and a gold snuffbox with the late count's portrait on it, which Pierre had commissioned from a miniaturist in Petersburg. The countess had been wanting this for a long time, but now she didn't feel like crying and so she looked at the portrait indifferently and focused instead on the card box.

"Thank you, my dear, you've cheered me up," she said, as she always did. "But best of all you've brought yourself back—this has been absolutely ridiculous. You really must scold your wife! What are we to do with her? Without you she's like a madwoman! She doesn't see anything, doesn't remember anything," she said with her usual phrases. "Look, Anna Timofeevna," she added to her companion, "see what a fine card box my son has brought me!"
Belova admired the presents and was delighted with her dress material.

Though Pierre, Natasha, Nicholas, Countess Mary, and Denisov had much to talk about that they couldn't discuss in front of the old countess—not that anything was hidden from her, but because she had fallen so far behind that if they had started talking about anything in front of her, they would have had to answer her irrelevant questions and repeat things she'd already been told. They would have had to explain that so-and-so was dead, or so-and-so was married, which she would forget again the next time—yet they sat at tea around the samovar in the drawing room, and Pierre answered the old countess's questions that were of no interest to anyone, telling her that Prince Vasili had aged, and that Countess Maria Alexeyevna sent her regards and remembered her kindly, and so on.

This kind of conversation, interesting to no one yet unavoidable, continued through teatime. All the grown-up members of the family were assembled around the round tea table where Sonya presided by the samovar. The children with their tutors and governesses had already had tea and could be heard in the next room. Everyone sat in their usual places at tea; Nicholas sat by the stove at a small table where his tea was passed to him; Milka, an old gray borzoi bitch, the daughter of the original Milka, with a face full of black spots, lay in an armchair beside him. Denisov, his curly hair now half-gray, his mustache and whiskers showing it too, sat next to Countess Mary with his general's unbuttoned tunic. Pierre sat between his wife and the old countess. He was telling them what he knew might interest the old lady and what she could understand. He talked about external social events and about those people who had once formed the circle of the old countess's contemporaries—who had once been a real, living, distinct group but who were now for the most part scattered over the world, finishing their earthly course like she was. But to the countess these contemporaries seemed to be the only serious and real society. Natasha could tell by Pierre's animation that his trip had been interesting and that he had much to say that he couldn't talk about in front of the old countess.

Denisov, not being a member of the family, didn't understand Pierre's caution and—being besides very interested in what was going on in Petersburg—kept urging Pierre to tell them about what had happened with the Semyonovsky regiment, or about Arakcheyev, or about the Bible Society. Pierre would occasionally get carried away and start talking, but Nicholas and Natasha always steered him back to the health of Prince Ivan Ivanovich and Countess Maria Antonovna.
"Well, and all this nonsense—Gossner and Tatarinova?" Denisov asked. "Is that really still going on?"
"Going on?" Pierre exclaimed. "Worse than ever! The Bible Society is practically running the government!"
"What's that, my dear?" asked the countess, who had finished her tea and was clearly looking for a reason to be cross after her meal. "What are you saying about the government? I don't understand."

"Well, you know, Mama," Nicholas put in, knowing how to translate things into his mother's language, "Prince Alexander Golitsyn has founded a society, and as a result he has a great deal of influence, they say."
"Arakcheyev and Golitsyn," Pierre said incautiously, "are practically the whole government! And what a government! They see treason everywhere and are frightened of everything."

"Well, and what's wrong with Prince Alexander? He's a most estimable man. I used to see him at Maria Antonovna's," said the countess in an offended tone; and still more offended that everyone remained silent, she went on: "Nowadays everyone finds fault with everything. A Bible society—well, what harm is there in that?" and she got up—everyone rising with her—and with a stern expression sailed back to her table in the sitting room.
The gloomy silence that followed was broken by the sounds of children's voices and laughter from the next room. Clearly some exciting game was going on in there.
"Finished, finished!" little Natasha's gleeful shout rose above them all.
Pierre exchanged glances with Countess Mary and Nicholas (he never lost sight of Natasha) and smiled happily.
"That's delightful music!" he said.
"It means Anna Makarovna has finished her stocking," said Countess Mary.

"Oh, I'll go and see," said Pierre, jumping up. "You know," he added, stopping at the door, "why I'm especially fond of that music? It's always the first thing that tells me all is well. Coming home today, the nearer I got to the house the more anxious I grew. When I came into the front hall and heard Andrusha laughing his head off upstairs, I knew everything was fine."
"I know! I know that feeling," said Nicholas. "But I can't go in there—those stockings are meant to be a surprise for me."
Pierre went in to the children, and the shouting and laughter grew even louder.

"Come on, Anna Makarovna," Pierre's voice could be heard saying, "come here into the middle of the room. At the word of command: 'One, two,' and when I say 'three'... You stand here, and you go in my arms—now then! One, two!..." said Pierre, and silence followed. "Three!" And an ecstatic roar of children's voices filled the room.

This meant two stockings, which Anna Makarovna used to knit simultaneously on the same needles by a secret technique known only to her, and which she would always triumphantly pull—one from inside the other—in the children's presence when they were finished.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter XIV
paragraphs: Soon after this the children came in to say good night. They kissed everyone; the tutors and governesses made their bows and went out. Only young Nicholas and his tutor Dessalles remained. Dessalles whispered to the boy to come downstairs.
"No, Monsieur Dessalles, I'll ask my aunt to let me stay," replied young Nicholas Bolkonsky, also in a whisper.
"Auntie, please let me stay," he said, going up to his aunt.
His face showed entreaty, excitement, and a kind of ecstasy. Countess Mary glanced at him and turned to Pierre.
"When you're here he can't tear himself away," she said.

"I'll bring him to you shortly, Monsieur Dessalles. Good night!" said Pierre, giving his hand to the Swiss tutor, and he turned to young Nicholas with a smile. "You and I haven't had a chance to talk yet... How like his father he's getting, Mary!" he added, turning to Countess Mary.
"Like my father?" the boy asked, blushing crimson and looking up at Pierre with bright, enraptured eyes.

Pierre nodded and went on with what he had been saying when the children interrupted. Countess Mary sat doing needlework; Natasha kept her eyes fixed on her husband. Nicholas and Denisov got up, asked for their pipes, smoked, fetched tea from Sonya—who sat wearily but stubbornly at the samovar—and asked Pierre questions. The curly-headed, sickly boy with his shining eyes sat unnoticed in a corner, turning his curly head with its delicate neck, poking out of his turndown collar, toward Pierre. Every now and then he would shiver and murmur something to himself, clearly experiencing some powerful new feeling.

The conversation turned to the current political gossip in which most people see the chief interest of domestic politics. Denisov, dissatisfied with the government because of his own career disappointments, was delighted to hear of the foolish things being done in Petersburg, and commented on Pierre's words in sharp, biting terms.

"Before, you had to be German—now you have to dance with Tatarinova and Madame Krudener, and read Eckhartshausen and the rest of that brotherhood. They should just let that fellow Bonaparte loose—he'd knock all this nonsense out of them! Can you imagine—giving command of the Semyonovsky regiment to a man like Schwartz!" he cried.

Nicholas, who didn't share Denisov's readiness to find fault with everything, also thought that discussing the government was very serious and weighty business, and the fact that A had been appointed Minister of This and B Governor General of That, and that the Emperor had said such-and-such and the minister something else, all seemed very important to him. And he thought it was his duty to take an interest in it and to question Pierre accordingly.

But Natasha, who knew all her husband's ways and ideas, could see that he had been wanting for some time—but unable—to steer the conversation to a different subject and express his own deeply felt idea, the one he'd gone to Petersburg to discuss with his new friend Prince Theodore. And she helped him with a question: what was his business with Prince Theodore about?
"What was it about?" asked Nicholas.

"Always the same thing," said Pierre, looking around at his listeners. "Everyone can see that things are going so badly they can't be allowed to continue, and that it's the duty of every decent person to fight against it as best they can."
"What can decent people do?" Nicholas asked, frowning slightly. "What can be done?"
"Well, this—"
"Come into my study," said Nicholas.

Natasha, who had long been expecting to be called to nurse the baby, now heard the nurse calling and went to the nursery. Countess Mary followed her. The men went into the study, and young Nicholas Bolkonsky slipped in after them unnoticed by his uncle and sat down at the desk in a dark corner by the window.
"Well, what would you do?" asked Denisov.
"Always some wild scheme," said Nicholas.

"Well, here it is," began Pierre, not sitting down but pacing the room, sometimes stopping short, gesturing, and speaking with a slight lisp. "The situation in Petersburg is this: the Emperor doesn't look into anything. He's surrendered himself entirely to mysticism." (Pierre could not forgive mysticism in anyone now.) "All he asks is peace, and the only people who can give him peace are the people who have no conscience, no honor—Magnitsky, Arakcheyev, and the rest. You'll agree that if you didn't look after your estates and only wanted peace, the more ruthless your steward was, the sooner you'd get it," he said, turning to Nicholas.
* Without faith or law.
"Well, what does that lead to?" said Nicholas.

"Well, everything is falling apart! Corruption in the courts; in the army, nothing but flogging, drilling, and Military Settlements. The people are tortured; enlightenment is crushed. Everything young and honest is being destroyed! Everyone can see this can't go on. The string is stretched too tight and must break," said Pierre—as people examining the actions of any government have always said, since governments first existed. "I told them one thing in Petersburg."
"Told whom?"

"Well, you know whom," said Pierre, with a meaningful look from under his brows. "Prince Theodore and the others. Encouraging culture and philanthropy is all very well, of course. The aim is excellent, but in the present circumstances something else is needed."
At that moment Nicholas noticed his nephew's presence. His face darkened and he went up to the boy.
"Why are you here?"

"Leave him be," said Pierre, taking Nicholas by the arm and continuing. "That's not enough, I told them. Something more is needed now. When you stand waiting for the overstrained string to snap at any moment, when everyone is expecting the inevitable catastrophe—as many people as possible must join hands as tightly as they can to resist the general disaster. Everything young and strong is being lured away and corrupted. One is tempted by women, another by honors, a third by ambition or money, and they go over to that camp. There's no independent, free people left, like you and me. I say: broaden the scope of the society; let the watchword be not just loyalty to the emperor and virtue, but independence and action."
Nicholas had left his nephew, irritably pushed an armchair into place, sat down, and listened to Pierre, coughing with displeasure and frowning more and more.
"But action toward what goal?" he cried. "And where do you stand in relation to the government?"

"We'd be assistants. The society needn't be secret if the government allows it. Far from being hostile to the government, it's a society of true conservatives—gentlemen in the full sense of the word. It exists only to prevent Pugachev from coming to slaughter my children and yours, and to prevent Arakcheyev from shipping me off to a military settlement. We join together with the single aim of the common good and general safety."
"Yes, but it's a secret society and therefore hostile and harmful, and can only cause trouble."

"Why? Did the Tugendbund, which saved Europe"—at that time no one yet ventured to say Russia had saved Europe—"do any harm? The Tugendbund is an alliance of virtue: it is love, mutual aid... it is what Christ preached on the Cross."

Natasha, who had come in during the conversation, looked joyfully at her husband. It wasn't what he was saying that pleased her—that didn't even interest her, because it all seemed extremely simple and she had known it all long ago (it seemed so to her because she knew the source it all came from—Pierre's whole soul). What delighted her was his animated, enthusiastic appearance.

The boy with the thin neck sticking out of his turndown collar—whom everyone had forgotten—gazed at Pierre with even greater rapturous joy. Every word of Pierre's burned into his heart, and with a nervous movement of his fingers he unconsciously broke the sealing wax and quill pens on his uncle's desk.
"It's not at all what you think. That's what the German Tugendbund was, and what I'm proposing."

"No, my friend! The Tugendbund is all very well for the sausage-eaters, but I don't understand it and can't even pronounce it," Denisov broke in with a loud, determined voice. "I agree that everything here is rotten and horrible, but the Tugendbund I don't understand. If you're not happy with things—a rebellion, now that I can understand! Count me in!"
* "I'm your man."

Pierre smiled; Natasha began to laugh; but Nicholas knitted his brows still more and set about proving to Pierre that no great upheaval was in the offing, and that all the danger Pierre spoke of existed only in his imagination. Pierre argued the opposite, and since his intellectual powers were greater and more resourceful, Nicholas soon felt at a loss. This made him still angrier, for he was inwardly aware that—not by reason but by something stronger than reason—the rightness of his view was beyond question.

"I'll tell you this," he said, standing up and trying with nervously twitching fingers to prop his pipe in a corner, finally giving up the attempt. "I can't prove it to you. You say everything here is rotten and there's going to be a revolution. I don't see it. But you also say the oath of allegiance is a conditional thing—and to that I reply: you're my best friend, you know that, but if you formed a secret society and started working against the government—whatever kind it might be—I'd know it was my duty to obey the government. And if Arakcheyev ordered me to lead a squadron against you and cut you down, I wouldn't hesitate for a second. Make of that what you will!"

An awkward silence followed. Natasha was the first to speak, defending her husband and attacking her brother. Her defense was weak and clumsy, but it achieved its purpose. The conversation resumed, no longer in the unpleasantly hostile tone of Nicholas's last words.
When they all got up to go in to supper, young Nicholas Bolkonsky went up to Pierre, pale and with shining, radiant eyes.
"Uncle Pierre, you... no... If Papa were alive... would he agree with you?" he asked.

And Pierre suddenly realized what a powerful, independent, and complex process of thought and feeling must have been going on inside this boy during the conversation. Remembering everything he had said, he regretted that the boy had heard him. He had to give an answer, however.
"Yes, I think so," he said reluctantly, and left the study.
The boy looked down and seemed for the first time to notice what he had done to the things on the desk. He flushed and went up to Nicholas.
"Uncle, forgive me—I did that... by accident," he said, pointing to the broken sealing wax and pens.
Nicholas started angrily.
"All right, all right," he said, throwing the pieces under the table.
And clearly suppressing his annoyance with difficulty, he turned away from the boy.
"You shouldn't have been here at all," he said.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter XV
paragraphs: The conversation at supper was not about politics or societies but turned to the subject Nicholas liked best—memories of 1812. Denisov started these, and Pierre was especially engaging and funny about them. The family separated on the friendliest terms.

After supper, Nicholas undressed in his study and gave instructions to the steward who had been waiting for him, then went to the bedroom in his dressing gown, where he found his wife still at her writing desk.
"What are you writing, Mary?" Nicholas asked.
Countess Mary blushed. She was afraid that what she was writing wouldn't be understood or approved by her husband.
She had wanted to hide it from him, but was at the same time glad he had caught her at it and that she would now have to tell him.
"A diary, Nicholas," she replied, handing him a blue exercise book filled with her firm, bold handwriting.
"A diary?" Nicholas repeated with a touch of irony, and took the book.
It was in French.

December 4. Today when Andrusha woke up he didn't want to get dressed, and Mademoiselle Louise sent for me. He was being naughty and stubborn. I tried threats, but he only got angrier. Then I took charge: I left him alone and began helping the nanny get the other children up, telling him I didn't love him. He was quiet for a long time, as if surprised. Then he rushed out to me in his nightshirt and was sobbing so hard that I couldn't calm him down for a long time. He was clearly most upset at having grieved me. Later, when I gave him his report card in the evening, he cried pitifully again as he kissed me. One can do anything with him through kindness.
"What's a 'report card'?" Nicholas asked.
"I've started giving the older children marks every evening, showing how they've behaved."

Nicholas looked into the radiant eyes gazing at him and continued turning pages and reading. Everything that seemed noteworthy about the children's characters or that suggested general principles of child-rearing was recorded in the diary. It was mostly small details, but they did not seem trivial to the mother or to the father who was now reading about his children for the first time.
Under the date "5" was this entry:

Mitya was naughty at the table. Papa said he should have no pudding. He got none, but looked so sadly and hungrily at the others while they ate! I think depriving children of sweets only makes them greedier. Must tell Nicholas.

Nicholas put down the book and looked at his wife. The radiant eyes gazed at him questioningly: would he approve or disapprove of her diary? There could be no doubt—not only of his approval but of his admiration for his wife.

"Perhaps it doesn't need to be done quite so methodically," Nicholas thought, "or even done at all." But this tireless, constant spiritual effort, aimed solely at the children's moral well-being, delighted him. If Nicholas could have analyzed his feelings, he would have found that his proud, tender love for his wife was grounded in this very sense of wonder at her inner life, at the lofty moral world that was almost beyond his reach, in which his wife always lived.

He was proud of her intelligence and goodness, recognized his own insignificance beside her in the spiritual realm, and rejoiced all the more that she—with such a soul—not only belonged to him but was part of himself.

"I completely approve, my dearest!" he said with a meaningful look. After a short pause he added: "And I behaved badly today. You weren't in the study. Pierre and I got into an argument, and I lost my temper. But he's impossible—such a child! I don't know what would happen to him if Natasha didn't keep him in line. Can you imagine what he went to Petersburg for... they're forming—"
"Yes, I know," said Countess Mary. "Natasha told me."

"Well, then you know," Nicholas went on, getting heated again at the mere memory of the discussion, "he wanted to convince me that it's every honest man's duty to go against the government, and that oaths of allegiance and duty... I'm sorry you weren't there. They all ganged up on me—Denisov and Natasha too... Natasha is ridiculous. She's got him completely under her thumb, but when it comes to an argument she has no mind of her own—she just parrots his words," Nicholas added, giving in to his irresistible urge to criticize people he loved. He forgot that what he said about Natasha could just as well be said word for word about himself in relation to his wife.
"Yes, I've noticed that," said Countess Mary.
"When I told him that duty and the oath come above everything, he started trying to prove God knows what! What a shame you weren't there—what would you have said?"

"As I see it, you were quite right, and I told Natasha so. Pierre says that everyone is suffering, being tortured and corrupted, and that it's our duty to help our neighbors. Of course he's right about that," said Countess Mary, "but he forgets that we have other, nearer duties—duties that God himself has set for us—and that we may risk ourselves but not our children."

"Yes, that's exactly what I said to him!" Nicholas put in, genuinely believing he had said it. "But they kept insisting on their view: love of one's neighbor and Christianity—and all this with young Nicholas sitting right there. He had slipped into my study and was smashing things to pieces."

"You know, Nicholas, I'm often worried about young Nicholas," said Countess Mary. "He's such an unusual boy. I'm afraid I neglect him in favor of my own children—we all have our children and our own family ties, while he has no one. He's always alone with his thoughts."

"Well, I don't think you need to blame yourself on his account. Everything the most devoted mother could do for a son, you've done and are doing for him. And of course I'm glad of it. He's a fine boy, a fine boy! This evening he listened to Pierre in a kind of trance. And do you know—when we stood up to go to supper, I looked over and he'd smashed everything on my desk to bits, and he told me about it himself right away. I've never known him to lie. A fine boy, really!" Nicholas repeated, pleased with his assessment.

"Still, I'm not the same as his own mother," said Countess Mary. "I feel that I'm not, and it troubles me. He's a wonderful boy, but I'm terribly afraid for him. It would be good for him to have companions."

"Well, it won't be long now. Next summer I'll take him to Petersburg," said Nicholas. "Yes, Pierre always was a dreamer and always will be," he continued, returning to the argument that had clearly upset him. "Well, what business is it of mine what goes on there—Arakcheyev's misconduct, and all the rest? What business was it of mine when we got married and I had so many debts that they were threatening to put me in prison? And what about your mother? She could never understand. And now—in a year or two I could show them Otradnoe! And if everything continues as it is, in another three years I'll have paid off all the debts, and then..."

Countess Mary wanted to tell him that man does not live by bread alone, and that he placed too much importance on these things. But she knew she must not say it and that it would be useless. She simply took his hand and kissed it. He took this as a sign of agreement and approval, and after a few moments of silent reflection went on thinking aloud.
"You know, Mary, today Elias Mitrofanych"—his overseer—"came back from the Tambov estate and told me they're already offering eighty thousand for the forest."

And with eager excitement Nicholas began talking about the possibility of buying Otradnoe back before long, adding: "Another ten years of life and I'll leave the children... in an excellent position."

Countess Mary listened to her husband and understood everything he told her. She knew that when he thought aloud like this he would sometimes ask what he'd been saying, and be annoyed if he noticed she'd been thinking about something else. But she had to make a considerable effort to pay attention, because what he said didn't interest her at all. She looked at him and—rather than thinking—felt something else entirely. She felt a submissive, tender love for this man who would never understand everything she understood, and she seemed to love him all the more for that, with a touch of passionate tenderness. Besides this feeling, which absorbed her entirely, she was also thinking about her children: she wasn't thinking about them, exactly, but feeling their existence—the need to watch over their health, to feed, to educate. She mentally counted them over, made sure she hadn't forgotten any, and felt at peace.

Sometimes it seemed to her that this difference between them came from the difference in their ages, but she also felt herself to be at fault and promised in her heart to do better, to accomplish the impossible—to love her husband, her children, all her relatives, and all people in this life, just as Christ loved mankind. Countess Mary's soul always strived toward the infinite, the eternal, and the absolute, and therefore could never be at peace. A stern expression of the lofty, secret suffering of a soul weighed down by the body appeared on her face. Nicholas looked at her. "My God! What will become of us if she dies, as I always fear when her face looks like that?" he thought, and standing before the icon he began to say his evening prayers.

chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter XVI
paragraphs: Natasha and Pierre, left alone, also began to talk—the way only a husband and wife can talk, that is, with extraordinary speed and clarity, understanding and expressing each other's thoughts in ways that defy all rules of logic, without premises, deductions, or conclusions, and in a totally unique manner. Natasha was so used to talking with her husband this way that Pierre's following an orderly logical train of thought was for her a sure sign something was wrong between them. When he began proving things, speaking calmly and reasonably, and when she, drawn in by his example, started doing the same, she knew it would lead to a quarrel.

From the moment they were alone together and Natasha came up to him with wide, happy eyes and quickly took his head and pressed it to her chest, saying, "Now you're all mine, mine! You won't escape!"—from that moment, a conversation began that defied all the laws of logic, if only because they talked about many completely different things at the same time. This simultaneous discussion of many topics, far from hindering a clear understanding, was the surest sign that they fully understood each other.

Just as in a dream everything is uncertain, unreasonable, and contradictory except the guiding feeling, so in this conversation—contrary to all laws of reason—the words themselves were not clear or consistent, but only the feeling that guided them.

Natasha told Pierre about her brother's life, about how she had suffered and felt dead inside during Pierre's absence, and how she was fonder than ever of Mary, and how Mary was better than her in every way. In saying this, Natasha was genuinely convinced that Mary was better, but she also expected Pierre to disagree with her—and he did.
Pierre, answering Natasha, told her how intolerable it had been for him to meet ladies at dinners and balls in Petersburg.
"I've completely lost the ability to talk to women," he said. "It was simply boring. Besides, I was very busy."
Natasha looked at him intently and went on:
"Mary is so wonderful," she said. "The way she understands children! It's as if she sees straight into their souls. Yesterday, for instance, Mitya was being naughty—"
"How much like his father he is," Pierre interjected.
Natasha knew why he mentioned Mitya's resemblance to Nicholas: the memory of his argument with his brother-in-law was unpleasant and he wanted to know what Natasha thought of it.
"Nicholas has the weakness of never agreeing with anything that isn't generally accepted. But I understand that you value what opens up a new path," she said, repeating words Pierre had once used.

"No, the main point is that for Nicholas, ideas and discussions are an amusement—almost a pastime," said Pierre. "He's building a library, for instance, and has made it a rule not to buy a new book until he's read the ones he already has—Sismondi, Rousseau, Montesquieu," he added with a smile. "You know how much I—" he began to soften, but Natasha interrupted, making it clear there was no need for that.
"So you say ideas are just a pastime for him..."
"Yes, and for me nothing else is serious. The whole time I was in Petersburg, I saw everyone as if in a dream. When I'm absorbed by a thought, everything else is just entertainment."
"Oh, I'm so sorry I wasn't there when you met the children," said Natasha. "Which one was most excited? Lisa, I'll bet."

"Yes," Pierre replied, and went on with what was on his mind. "Nicholas says we shouldn't think. But I can't help it. Not to mention that in Petersburg I felt—I can tell you this—the whole thing would have fallen apart without me. Everyone was pulling in his own direction. But I managed to bring them all together, and then my idea is so clear and simple. I'm not saying we should act against this or that. We may be wrong. What I say is: let those who love what's right join hands, and let there be one banner—active virtue. Prince Sergei is a fine man and smart."

Natasha would have had no doubt about the greatness of Pierre's idea, but one thing bothered her. "Can a man so important and necessary to society also be my husband? How did that happen?" She wanted to express this doubt. "Now, who could have decided that he was really so much cleverer than all the rest?" she asked herself, and mentally reviewed all the people Pierre especially respected. Judging by his accounts, there was no one he respected more than Platon Karataev.
"Do you know what I'm thinking about?" she asked. "About Platon Karataev. Would he have approved of you now, do you think?"
Pierre was not at all surprised by this question. He understood his wife's way of thinking.
"Platon Karataev?" he repeated, and thought about it, clearly trying sincerely to imagine Karataev's opinion on the subject. "He wouldn't have understood... yet maybe he would."
"I love you terribly!" Natasha suddenly said. "Terribly, terribly!"

"No, he wouldn't have approved," said Pierre, after reflection. "What he would have approved of is our family life. He always wanted so much to see harmony, happiness, and peace in everything, and I would have been proud to show him our life. There you are—you talk about being apart. But you have no idea what special feeling I have for you after a separation..."
"Yes, and also—" Natasha began.
"No, it's not that. I never stop loving you. And one couldn't love more, but this is something special... Well, of course—" He didn't finish, because their eyes met and said the rest.

"What nonsense it is," Natasha suddenly exclaimed, "about honeymoons, and that the greatest happiness comes at the beginning! On the contrary, now is the best time of all. If only you wouldn't go away! Do you remember how we used to quarrel? And it was always my fault. Always. And what we quarreled about—I don't even remember."
"Always the same thing," Pierre said with a smile. "Jealo—"
"Don't say it! I can't stand it!" Natasha cried, and a cold, vindictive glitter flashed in her eyes. "Did you see her?" she added after a pause.
"No, and if I had I wouldn't have recognized her."
They were silent for a while.

"Oh, do you know? While you were talking in the study, I was watching you," Natasha began, clearly wanting to chase away the cloud that had come over them. "You look just like your son—like two peas in a pod," she said, meaning her little boy. "Oh, it's time to go to him... My milk must be coming in... But I feel sorry to leave you."

They were silent for a few seconds. Then suddenly, turning to each other at the same time, they both began to speak. Pierre began with self-satisfaction and enthusiasm, Natasha with a quiet, happy smile. Having interrupted each other, they both stopped to let the other go first.
"No, what were you going to say? Go on, go on."
"No, you go on. I was just talking nonsense," said Natasha.

Pierre finished what he had begun. It was the continuation of his self-satisfied reflections on his success in Petersburg. At that moment it seemed to him that he had been chosen to give a new direction to the whole of Russian society and to the whole world.

"I only wanted to say that ideas with great consequences are always simple. My whole idea is that if evil people are united and working together as a force, then honest people need to do the same. It's as simple as that."
"Yes."
"And what were you going to say?"
"Oh, nothing. Just nonsense."
"No, tell me anyway."

"Oh, it's nothing, just a trifle," said Natasha, smiling even more brightly. "I only wanted to tell you about Petya: today the nurse came to take him from me, and he laughed, shut his eyes, and clung to me—he must have thought he was hiding. He's so sweet! There he is, crying. Well, goodbye!" And she left the room.

Meanwhile, downstairs in young Nicholas Bolkonsky's bedroom, a lamp was burning as usual. (The boy was afraid of the dark and they couldn't cure him of it.) Dessalles lay sleeping, propped up on four pillows, his Roman nose emitting sounds of rhythmic snoring. Young Nicholas, who had just woken up in a cold sweat, sat up in bed with wide-open eyes. He had been woken by a terrible dream. In the dream, he and Uncle Pierre were marching at the head of a huge army, wearing helmets like the ones illustrated in his edition of Plutarch. The army was made of white, slanting lines that filled the air like spiderwebs in autumn—what Dessalles called "the threads of the Virgin Mary." Ahead of them was glory, the same as those threads but somewhat denser. They—he and Pierre—were borne along lightly and joyfully, closer and closer to their goal. Suddenly the threads began to weaken and tangle; it grew heavy. And Uncle Nicholas stood before them in a stern, threatening posture.

"Have you done this?" he said, pointing to some broken sealing wax and pens. "I loved you, but Arakcheyev has given me orders and I will kill the first of you who moves forward." Young Nicholas turned to look at Pierre, but Pierre was no longer there. In his place was his father—Prince Andrew—and his father had no form or shape, but he was there, and seeing him, Nicholas felt the weakness of love: he felt limp, boneless, and formless. His father caressed him and pitied him. But Uncle Nicholas advanced closer and closer. A terrible fear gripped the boy, and he woke up.

"My father!" he thought. (Though there were two good portraits of Prince Andrew in the house, Nicholas never imagined him in human form.) "My father was with me and comforted me. He approved of me and of Uncle Pierre. Whatever Uncle Pierre says, I will do it. Mucius Scaevola burned his hand. But why shouldn't the same things happen in my life? I know people want me to study and I will study. But someday I'll stop studying, and then I'll do it. I ask only one thing of God: that the same thing happens to me as happened to the men in Plutarch. And I will do even better. Everyone will know me, love me, and admire me." And suddenly his chest heaved with sobs and he began to cry.
"Are you ill?" he heard Dessalles's voice ask.
"No," Nicholas answered, and lay back on his pillow.

"He is kind and good, and I'm fond of him!" he thought about Dessalles. "But Uncle Pierre! Oh, what a wonderful man he is! And my father? Oh, Father, Father! Yes, I will do something that even he would be proud of..."

chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter I
paragraphs: History is the life of nations and of humanity. To capture and put into words—to directly describe—the life of humanity or even of a single nation seems impossible.

The ancient historians all used one and the same method to describe and capture the apparently elusive life of a people. They described the activities of individuals who ruled the people, and treated those activities as representing the activity of the whole nation.

The question of how individuals made nations act according to their will, and what guided the will of those individuals themselves, the ancients answered by invoking a divinity that subjected nations to the will of a chosen man and guided that man's will toward a predetermined end.
For the ancients, these questions were resolved by belief in the direct involvement of God in human affairs.
Modern history, in theory, rejects both these principles.

It would seem that, having rejected the ancients' belief in humanity's subjection to God and in a predetermined goal toward which nations are led, modern history should study not the displays of power but the causes that produce it. But modern history has not done this. Having rejected the theoretical views of the ancients, it follows them in practice.

Instead of men endowed with divine authority and directly guided by God's will, modern history has given us either heroes with extraordinary, superhuman abilities, or simply men of various kinds—from monarchs to journalists—who lead the masses. Instead of the ancients' divinely appointed goals for nations—the greatness of Rome, Greece, or God's chosen people—modern history has set up its own goals: the welfare of the French, German, or English people, or—in its highest abstraction—the welfare and civilization of all humanity, by which it usually means the peoples occupying a small northwestern corner of a large continent.

Modern history has rejected the ancients' beliefs without replacing them with a new understanding, and the logic of the situation has forced historians—after apparently rejecting the divine authority of kings and the "destiny" of the ancients—to arrive at the same conclusion by a different road: to recognize (1) that nations are led by individual people, and (2) that there exists a certain goal toward which nations and humanity are being guided.
All the works of modern historians, from Gibbon to Buckle, despite their apparent disagreements and seeming novelty of outlook, rest on those two old, inescapable assumptions.

In the first place, the historian describes the activity of individuals who in his opinion directed humanity. One historian considers only monarchs, generals, and ministers as such people, while another includes orators, scholars, reformers, philosophers, and poets as well. But all historians agree that these individuals expressed the will of their time, and that their activity was the direction in which the historical movement flowed.

In 1789 a ferment arises in Paris; it grows, spreads, and takes the form of a movement of peoples from west to east. Several times it surges eastward and collides with a counter-movement from east to west. In 1812 it reaches its extreme limit—Moscow—and then, with remarkable symmetry, a counter-movement occurs from east to west, pulling along the peoples of Central Europe. The counter-movement reaches the starting point—Paris—and subsides.

During those twenty years, an immense number of fields were left untilled, houses were burned, trade changed direction, millions of people migrated, were impoverished or enriched, and millions of Christian men who professed the law of love slaughtered one another.

What does all this mean? Why did it happen? What made those people burn houses and kill their fellow men? What were the causes of these events? What force made people act this way? These are the instinctive, simple, and most natural questions humanity asks when it encounters the monuments and traditions of that bygone era.
For answers to these questions, common sense turns to the science of history, whose purpose is to help nations and humanity know themselves.

If history had kept the ancients' conception, it would have said: God, to reward or punish His people, gave Napoleon power and directed his will toward the fulfillment of divine purposes. And that answer would have been clear and complete. One could believe or disbelieve in the divine significance of Napoleon, but for anyone who believed in it, all of that era's history would have been comprehensible, and there would be no contradictions.
But modern history cannot give that answer. Science does not accept the ancients' belief in direct divine intervention in human affairs, and therefore history must provide different answers.
Modern history, answering these questions, says: you want to know what this movement means, what caused it, and what force produced these events? Listen:

"Louis XIV was a very proud and self-confident man; he had such-and-such mistresses and such-and-such ministers, and he ruled France badly. His successors were weak men and they too ruled France badly. And they had certain favorites and certain mistresses. Furthermore, at that time certain men wrote certain books. At the end of the eighteenth century, about twenty men got together in Paris and started saying that all men are equal and free. This led people all over France to start attacking and killing each other. They killed the king and many others. At that time there was a man of genius in France—Napoleon. He conquered everyone everywhere—that is, he killed a lot of people—because he was a very great genius. And for some reason he went to kill Africans, and killed them so well, and was so cunning and clever, that when he returned to France he ordered everyone to obey him. And they all obeyed him. Having become an Emperor, he went to kill people in Italy, Austria, and Prussia. And there too he killed a great many. In Russia there was Emperor Alexander, who decided to restore order in Europe and therefore fought against Napoleon. But in 1807 he suddenly made friends with Napoleon, then in 1811 quarreled with him again, and again they went about killing a great many people. Napoleon led six hundred thousand men into Russia and captured Moscow; then he suddenly ran away from Moscow, and Emperor Alexander—aided by the advice of Stein and others—united Europe to march against the destroyer of its peace. All Napoleon's allies suddenly became his enemies; and this force marched against Napoleon, who had raised fresh forces. The allies defeated Napoleon, entered Paris, forced Napoleon to abdicate, and sent him to the island of Elba, without depriving him of his title of Emperor and showing him every respect, though five years before and one year later they all considered him a brigand and an outlaw. Then Louis XVIII—who until then had been an object of ridicule to both the French and the allies—began to reign. As for Napoleon, after shedding tears before the Old Guard, he abdicated and went into exile. Then skillful statesmen and diplomats (particularly Talleyrand, who managed to sit down before anyone else in a particular chair at a particular reception, thereby enlarging the borders of France) held talks in Vienna and by those talks made the nations happy or unhappy. Then the diplomats and monarchs nearly quarreled and were about to order their armies to kill each other once more; but at that moment Napoleon arrived back in France with a battalion, and the French, who had been hating him, all immediately submitted. But the allied monarchs were displeased at this and again went to fight the French. And the genius Napoleon was defeated and taken to the island of St. Helena, having suddenly been recognized as a robber. And there the exile, separated from his dear ones and from his beloved France, died a slow death on a rock and bequeathed his great deeds to posterity. But in Europe a reaction set in, and the sovereigns all took to oppressing their peoples again."

It would be wrong to think this is ironic—a caricature of historical accounts. On the contrary, it is a very mild rendering of the contradictory and inconclusive answers that all historians give, from the authors of memoirs and national histories to the writers of universal histories and the new cultural historians.
The strangeness and absurdity of these answers comes from the fact that modern history, like a deaf man, answers questions no one has asked.

If the purpose of history is to describe the movement of humanity and of nations, the first question—without answering which everything else becomes incomprehensible—is: What is the power that moves peoples? To this, modern history laboriously tells us that Napoleon was a very great genius, or that Louis XIV was very proud, or that certain writers wrote certain books.

All that may be so, and humanity is ready to agree. But it is not what was asked. All that would be interesting if we accepted a divine power, based on itself and always consistent, directing nations through Napoleons, Louises, and writers. But we do not accept such a power, and therefore, before talking about Napoleons, Louises, and writers, we need to show the connection between these individuals and the movement of nations.
If some other force has replaced divine power, then it should be explained what this new force consists of, because the whole interest of history lies precisely in that force.

History seems to assume that this force is self-evident and known to everyone. But despite every desire to regard it as known, anyone who reads many historical works cannot help doubting whether this new force—so differently understood by historians themselves—is really so well known to everyone.
